title: New Brunswick screw
description: In New Brunswick, the insulator is secured by only one protruding screw

title: Vancouver Island RPM
description: Those buried RPM that are very common in the US are very rare in Canada. They are located 95% in Vancouver Island and 5% in Vancouver itself.

title: New Brunswick wooden bridges
description: The distinctive wooden truss bridges you see in the picture are found almost exclusively in New Brunswick.

title: Wooden sign posts
description: Canada still uses a lot of wooden posts for road signs, while the US almost always uses metal ones. A plain wooden post under a yellow warning sign is a good hint for Canada over the US.

title: Rumble strips without breaks
description: Edge rumble strips with regular gaps in them are almost always US. Canada has rumble strips too, but they run continuously without breaks.

title: Temperatures in Celsius
description: Signs showing temperatures in degrees Celsius, such as icy-road warnings with 0°C, rule out the US, which uses Fahrenheit.

title: Canadian Tire
description: Canadian Tire, with its red triangle and green maple leaf, is a very common Canadian brand. Many gas stations carry the logo too.

title: The big Canadian banks
description: TD, RBC, BMO, CIBC and Scotiabank are the big Canadian banks and appear in every town. Other Canada-only chains: Tim Hortons, Loblaws, No Frills, Sobeys, Shoppers Drug Mart, Rexall, Sport Chek, Mark's, Harvey's.

title: Chains that rule out Canada
description: Spotting Target, Kmart, Barnes & Noble, White Castle, Sonic, Carl's Jr, Whataburger, Dunkin' Donuts, Dollar General, Family Dollar, Walgreens or CVS means you are not in Canada. 7-Eleven is rare in Canada.

title: Trans-Canada Highway shield
description: The Trans-Canada Highway is marked with a white maple leaf on a green shield. It crosses every province; the province name is sometimes written on the shield.

title: Yellow buried cable markers
description: Markers for buried cables are found everywhere in Canada, which makes them useful on rural roads. Yellow ones are the norm in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, and common in Saskatchewan. Red ones belong to the prairies and are rare elsewhere.

title: Blue photocell on street lamps
description: Canadian street lamps carry a small blue photocell on top of the head. It is much less common in most other countries.

title: Blue rural address numbers
description: Rural address numbers on a small blue plate on a post are extremely common in Quebec and Atlantic Canada, where they are always blue. They are rare west of Ontario. Nova Scotia also likes blue mailboxes.

title: Gen 4 black car
description: Canada's Gen 4 black car, with its dark taillight visible below the camera. Found, from most to least common, in Manitoba, northern Ontario and Nova Scotia, with some spillover into the Ottawa region.

title: Dark poles in the west, light in the east
description: Utility poles in British Columbia and the west tend to be darker with fewer knots. Poles in Eastern Canada are lighter in colour with more knots in the wood.

title: Siding houses in Atlantic Canada
description: In Atlantic Canada most houses are clad in horizontal wood siding, often brightly coloured. Brick houses, so common in southern Ontario, are rare out east.

title: Ontario plates
description: Ontario has front and rear plates. Blurred personal plates look white with hints of blue; from 2020 a new fully blue plate appears, and veteran plates show a big red circle through the blur. Similar to BC plates, but the landscape tells them apart.

title: Ontario area codes
description: Ontario area codes: 416/647/437 Toronto, 905/289/365 around Toronto and Niagara, 519/226/548 the southwest, 613/343 the east, 705/249 central and northeastern Ontario, 807 the northwest. 807 means Thunder Bay or the far northwest.

title: Black strip under Ontario signs
description: Around half of Ontario's speed and regulatory signs carry a black strip at the bottom, saying for instance 'km/h' or 'begins'. Unique to Ontario.

title: Green electrical boxes
description: Green electrical boxes with yellow numbers, a circle and a danger sticker, common in Ontario residential areas. In southern Ontario suburbs a brown and a green box often stand side by side.

title: Posts with coloured caps at intersections
description: Posts with a yellow or orange cap are found occasionally at rural intersections in southern Ontario, sometimes on a full utility pole. A handful exist in Quebec.

title: Orange construction lines
description: During construction Ontario sometimes paints the lane lines orange to reduce the need for pylons.

title: Yellow hydrants in Ontario
description: Ontario generally uses yellow-body fire hydrants, with nozzle colours that vary. The body colour is the most reliable clue; a few regions use red instead.

title: Red hydrants in the Golden Horseshoe
description: Hamilton, Halton, Peel and Niagara mostly use red-body hydrants, unlike the yellow ones in the rest of Ontario. Sault Ste. Marie and Fort Frances also use red.

title: Concession and sideroad signs
description: Standard rural road signs in Ontario are green with this font, often naming a 'Concession' or a 'Sideroad'. Big cities such as Toronto, Ottawa, Niagara and Kitchener use blue.

title: Ontario tourism signs
description: This blue and white 'Ontario' destination sign pointing to points of interest is unique to and common in Ontario.

title: Square perforated sign posts
description: Ontario mostly uses square metal sign posts with small holes. Other provinces use round or solid posts more often.

title: Natural gas pipeline warnings
description: This style of natural gas pipeline warning sign is unique to Ontario and often found on the side of rural roads.

title: Adopt a Road signs
description: Blue 'Adopt a Road' signs naming a local group or town are specific to Ontario.

title: Black mobile billboards
description: Black portable advertising signs with bright letters are most common in Ontario and often include a phone number with its area code.

title: Wooden backs of info signs
description: The backs of information signs in rural Ontario are recognisable: wooden posts and a plain back. Quebec almost always uses metal posts.

title: Gentle curve-ahead arrow
description: Ontario's curve-ahead sign bends noticeably less than Quebec's, which has a much sharper curve.

title: County road number on street signs
description: Green street signs carrying the county name and road number below are distinctive of southern Ontario, mostly the southwest (here, Brant county).

title: Emergency numbers on road signs
description: Some green information signs carry small numbers along the bottom to help emergency vehicles. Only found in Ontario.

title: Oblique road grid
description: Ontario's road grid is almost always tilted, not aligned with the cardinal directions, whereas the prairie grid runs perfectly north-south. Useful for Ontario/prairie toss-ups.

title: Steel guardrails with blue tops
description: Some of Ontario's wooden wire guardrails are being replaced by steel guardrails with blue post tops.

title: Two-rib tilted insulator
description: This exact tilted insulator with two ribs, on its tilted attachment, is definitively Ontario.

title: Crossarm with three tall ribbed insulators
description: A crossarm carrying three tall, tilted, ribbed insulators should only be Ontario. The tall ribbed style alone is most common in Ontario, then BC, then Newfoundland.

title: Secondary crossarms
description: A second, lower crossarm is mainly found in Ontario and BC; you should never see one out east.

title: Railway poles with many insulators
description: Near railway tracks, poles with many crossarms and a large number of insulators are distinctive of Ontario.

title: Four mini insulators
description: A crossarm with four small 'mini' insulators is exclusive to Ontario.

title: Mini insulators
description: Small, short insulators like these are most common in Ontario and Manitoba, sometimes Saskatchewan, rarely Alberta.

title: Stubby ribbed 'UFO' insulator
description: A single stubby ribbed insulator on top of the pole with no crossarm is found in Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland. Within Ontario it is mostly in the far southwest.

title: GTA suburban lamp posts
description: This lamp post is abundant in southern Ontario suburbs, especially around Toronto. The decorative top is not always there: the octagonal post with its spotty colour is the real giveaway, often with a yellow vertical sticker.

title: Downtown Toronto lamp
description: This curved lamp is specific to downtown Toronto.

title: Vertical yellow pole numbers
description: The most common and distinctive Ontario pole marking: yellow tags with black numbers read vertically. Colourful dots and grey vertical numbers are common too.

title: Orange flags on wires
description: Small orange flags and yellow circles hung on power lines are found in Ontario and Quebec.

title: King's Highway crown shields
description: Ontario's provincial highways use a white shield topped by a crown. The 400-series are freeways; the main series runs 2-148.

title: County road trapezoid shields
description: County roads in southern Ontario use a white inverted trapezoid with the county or region name. Numbers repeat across county lines. In the north, secondary highways 500-699 use an upright trapezoid instead.

title: 407 ETR toll highway
description: The 407 ETR is Ontario's only toll highway and the only significant one in Canada. Look for its blue ETR signs and gantries with plate cameras.

title: HOV diamond lanes
description: HOV lanes marked with painted diamonds are common on Toronto-area freeways such as the 400-series and the QEW. They also appear around Vancouver, Montreal and on some Ottawa bridges.

title: Yellow strip on exit signs
description: Only in Ontario do exit signs have a yellow bottom section with black arrows showing which lanes exit.

title: Big red light on top
description: Ontario's traffic lights have a top red lens that is larger than the other two. Some provinces use similar yellow housings but the larger red is unique to Ontario.

title: Yellow pedestrian signals
description: This style of yellow pedestrian walking signal is unique to Ontario.

title: Green rural address numbers
description: Around 80% of rural address numbers in Ontario are green, which is close to unique. Manitoba rarely has green ones; elsewhere in the east they are blue.

title: Claybelt farmland
description: Apart from the south, the only big farming area of Ontario is the Claybelt around Temiskaming and Cochrane: wheat and canola, little corn. Its coverage often has a bright sun to the south.

title: Large maple trees in the south
description: Within Ontario, big maple trees are only found in the south.

title: Prairie-like southwest Ontario
description: The far southwest of Ontario near Sarnia and Windsor is flat farmland that can resemble the prairies. Hills increase to the north and trees to the east.

title: Snowy Gen 3 in northwestern Ontario
description: Northwestern Ontario has a lot of distinctive Gen 3 coverage with snow and sun glare.

title: Brick suburbs of southern Ontario
description: Southern Ontario suburbs are very recognisable: whole neighbourhoods of brick houses like this are not found anywhere else in Canada. Northern Ontario uses more siding.

title: Square roof vents
description: Square roof vents are very distinctive of Ontario. Quebec uses larger rectangular vents in the same place.

title: Trapezoid accent bricks
description: Trapezoid accent bricks above windows and garages are a common feature of southern Ontario houses.

title: Driveways cut by sidewalks
description: Sidewalks cutting across driveways are extremely common in southern Ontario and very rare anywhere else.

title: Gable windows
description: A window in the gable is a staple of southern Ontario houses. Quebec will often use a gable vent in the same place.

title: V-pattern sewer grates
description: The most common sewer grate in Ontario has this V-shaped pattern, exclusive to the province; very rare exceptions exist in the prairies.

title: St. Lawrence Lowlands farms
description: The farms of southern Ontario are distinctive: white-topped round grain silos and gambrel-roofed barns. Similar farms exist in the far southwest of Quebec, but Ontario has more silos and fancier roofs.

title: Bilingual signs in Ontario
description: Bilingual English-French signage in Ontario is mostly found around Ottawa and Sudbury, and especially in the region east of Sudbury.

title: Wind turbines near Lake Huron
description: Wind turbines in Ontario are almost exclusive to the southwest, especially along the Lake Huron shore.

title: Roundabouts in Ontario
description: There are no roundabouts in northern Ontario. They cluster around Kitchener, London and the Ottawa region.

title: LCBO liquor stores
description: Each province runs its own liquor store chain. LCBO is only found in Ontario.

title: ONroute service centres
description: ONroute service centres are only found along highways 401 and 400. Their gas stations carry the Canadian Tire logo.

title: Ottawa street signs
description: Ottawa street signs are blue and bilingual, with a circular logo. Ottawa almost always has bilingual signage.

title: Blue-capped hydrants in Ottawa
description: Ottawa hydrants keep the standard Ontario yellow body but have a distinctive blue cap.

title: OC Transpo bus stops
description: Ottawa bus stop signs are distinctive: white with a red maple leaf header and the 560-1000 number.

title: Bent metal posts in Ottawa
description: Ottawa posts are sometimes a single piece of bent metal, whereas the rest of Ontario mostly uses dotted square posts.

title: TTC bus stops
description: Toronto bus stops carry the very recognisable red TTC transit logo.

title: Toronto street signs
description: Most Toronto street signs follow this blue style with a white border and a neighbourhood name on top.

title: Toronto logo on bins
description: Most garbage bins in Toronto carry the city's logo.

title: CN Tower
description: The CN Tower is Toronto's main landmark and can be seen from surprisingly far away.

title: Stop signs mounted sideways in Hamilton
description: In Hamilton stop signs are often attached perpendicular to a post or another sign, which is rare elsewhere in Ontario.

title: Blue 'area' strip on speed signs
description: Speed signs in Hamilton often have a blue 'AREA' strip. It occurs elsewhere in Ontario but is especially common in Hamilton.

title: Sleeping Giant from Thunder Bay
description: This large flat-topped mountain to the south is the best way to recognise Thunder Bay and is visible from many places in the city. A long peninsula is also visible offshore.

title: Gloomy Thunder Bay coverage
description: Most coverage in Thunder Bay is dark and gloomy with bare trees. Compared with Sudbury it looks poorer, colder and has more cracked roads.

title: Pale yellow hydrants in Thunder Bay
description: Thunder Bay hydrants are a lighter yellow than the usual Ontario yellow, with fully yellow nozzles.

title: Thunder Bay street signs
description: Thunder Bay street signs have a small metal strip with two screws at the bottom and sit on recognisable square wooden posts.

title: Green bus stops in Thunder Bay
description: Thunder Bay bus stop signs are this unusual green colour.

title: Fire route numbers in Niagara
description: Street signs in Niagara sometimes carry fire route numbers.

title: Octagonal concrete poles in Niagara
description: Suburban poles in Niagara often use an octagonal concrete design.

title: Blue buses in Niagara
description: Niagara uses blue bus stop signs and blue buses.

title: Smokestacks around Sudbury
description: Very tall smokestacks stand just west of Sudbury.

title: Sudbury bus signs
description: Sudbury bus stop signs are recognisable and found all over the city.

title: 'S' pole tags in Sudbury
description: Sudbury uses thick yellow utility pole markings that always start with 'S'.

title: Red hydrants in Sault Ste. Marie
description: Sault Ste. Marie is one of the few Ontario cities with red hydrants, here with a blue top.

title: Sault Ste. Marie street signs
description: Sault Ste. Marie uses blue street signs with a white top and bottom edge.

title: Black-centred traffic lights
description: Traffic lights in Sault Ste. Marie have a black middle.

title: Kenora hydrants
description: Kenora hydrants look like this and always have a red snow pole. Kenora is hilly with exposed rock even on residential streets, and uses blue house numbers instead of Ontario's green.

title: Blue-nozzle hydrants in London
description: London's yellow hydrants almost always have blue nozzles.

title: London pole tags
description: London pole tags are black and start with 'SW' or 'T'. SW seems more common in the northeast of the city.

title: London Transit buses
description: London Transit buses carry a recognisable 'LT' symbol.

title: London sewer grates
description: London has its own sewer grate design.

title: Orange-topped hydrants in Sarnia
description: A yellow hydrant with an orange top and green sticker is found in Sarnia and other towns of the far southwest.

title: Windsor hydrants
description: Around 75% of Windsor's hydrants look like this: yellow with a blue top.

title: Kitchener-Waterloo bus stops
description: Kitchener and Waterloo have these recognisable GRT bus stop signs.

title: Thick white borders in Kitchener
description: Kitchener and Waterloo street signs have extra thick white borders.

title: Red hydrants in Fort Frances
description: Fort Frances is one of the few Ontario towns with red hydrants, with a snow pole.

title: Address ranges on Timmins signs
description: Timmins street signs are green and show the address ranges in the corners.

title: Gingerbread trim in Brooklin
description: Decorations at the end of roof ridges and dormers are extremely common in the town of Brooklin, Durham Region.

title: Brooklin street signs
description: Brooklin has its own black heritage street sign on all-black posts, which makes the town instantly recognisable.

title: Historic houses of Durham
description: Durham Region has many near-identical historic brick houses with alternating accent bricks on the corners and a decorated cornice under the gutters.

title: Uxbridge street signs
description: This blue and white street sign labelled 'TWP Uxbridge' is unique to the township of Uxbridge.

title: Durham hydrants
description: Durham hydrants are standard Ontario yellow with a black nozzle. Hydrants on private property must be red with a black storz, so red ones appear in plazas and parking lots.

title: Durham Region Transit
description: Durham Region Transit's green and white bus stop sign.

title: Port Perry street signs
description: Port Perry has its own black heritage street signs reading 'Old Port Perry'.

title: Blue street signs in Durham
description: Durham almost always uses blue street signs, whereas green is the most common across Ontario.

title: Toronto back lanes
description: In dense lower-income areas of Toronto you will find lanes of garages like this.

title: Toronto Islands trekker
description: The Toronto Islands have a lot of Gen 2 trekker coverage on narrow brick or stone walking paths between houses.

title: Downtown Burlington
description: Downtown Burlington has traffic lights with black insides and its own blue heritage street sign.

title: Burlington hydrants
description: Burlington and the surrounding area consistently use this red hydrant with a cream top and black nozzle.

title: White outlines on Oakville signs
description: Oakville always uses a white outline on its green street signs.

title: Blue nozzles in Halton
description: Apart from Burlington, most of Halton Region uses red hydrants with blue nozzles.

title: Black nozzle in Milton
description: The town of Milton uses a black front nozzle on its red hydrants.

title: Plain blue signs in Halton
description: Halton Region consistently uses plain blue street signs outside downtowns.

title: Peel hydrants
description: The whole Peel Region - Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon - very consistently uses red hydrants with a silver top and blue nozzles.

title: Brampton and Caledon street signs
description: Brampton and Caledon use green street signs with a white border.

title: Mississauga street signs
description: Mississauga uses plain blue street signs.

title: Barrie street signs
description: Barrie always puts white lines on the top and bottom of its green street signs. Its hydrants are yellow with a snow pole.

title: Barrie downtown district signs
description: Barrie's downtown neighbourhoods use black street signs naming the district at the top and bottom.

title: Orillia hydrants
description: Orillia always uses red hydrants with a green top and a snow pole.

title: Penetanguishene street signs
description: Penetanguishene has bilingual street signs with a ship logo.

title: Bracebridge hydrants
description: Bracebridge hydrants are red with blue nozzles and a red marker sign on a pole.

title: Gravenhurst signs and hydrants
description: Gravenhurst uses blue street signs and yellow hydrants with a light blue top. The rest of rural Muskoka uses green signs and yellow hydrants.

title: York Region hydrants by town
description: York Region hydrants change from town to town: Richmond Hill red with a light blue top, Aurora and Newmarket red, Markham and Vaughan yellow, the rest of York pale yellow with a black nozzle.

title: Thick-based lamps in Stouffville
description: Whitchurch-Stouffville uses almost only these lamps with a thick base.

title: Township names on Hastings signs
description: Street signs in Hastings County are unique: they always carry the township name and a county road number.

title: Belleville sign clamps
description: The clamps holding street signs in downtown Belleville are unique.

title: Belleville hydrants
description: Belleville uses yellow hydrants with a green top and green nozzles, unique and consistent.

title: Kingston hydrants
description: Kingston hydrants are yellow with a blue top and blue nozzles, consistent and reliable.

title: Kingston pole tags
description: Kingston poles carry small silver oval number tags, consistently.

title: Black traffic lights in downtown Kingston
description: Downtown Kingston has unique black traffic light poles and black heritage lamps.

title: Kingston street signs
description: Kingston street signs are green with a thin white border.

title: Wolfe Island wind turbines
description: Wolfe Island near Kingston is covered in wind turbines. Its signage uses an old square font similar to Prince Edward County and Quebec.

title: Quebec plates
description: Quebec requires no front plate. Plates are white, sometimes with a delicate blue tint in the upper corners.

title: Quebec area codes
description: Quebec area codes: 514/438 Montreal island, 450/579 around Montreal, 418/581 Quebec City and the east, 819/873 the west and north.

title: Gen 2 is rare in Quebec
description: Gen 2 coverage is extremely rare in Quebec, whereas it is quite common in Ontario.

title: Laurentians north of the St. Lawrence
description: North of the St. Lawrence River lies the Laurentian range. The mountains get taller to the east, especially north of Quebec City.

title: Low Appalachian hills south of the river
description: South of the St. Lawrence the end of the Appalachians gives smaller hills than the Laurentians north of the river.

title: Horizontal traffic lights
description: Quebec uses horizontal traffic lights, most commonly with a black housing.

title: High T crossarm, parallel transformer
description: This pole top is most common in Quebec and New Brunswick: the crossarm sits very high, almost touching the top, like a 'T'. Nova Scotia's is lower, like a 't'. Quebec mounts the transformer parallel; New Brunswick perpendicular.

title: L-shaped pole tops
description: This L-shaped pole top is found throughout Quebec but is most common on the Gaspé Peninsula. It also appears in British Columbia.

title: Ground wires into a covered block
description: In Quebec it is common for wires running down a pole to feed into a covered cement block at the base.

title: Strongly curved lamp arms
description: Quebec lamp arms curve more than in other provinces. Nova Scotia and Newfoundland also mostly use curved arms; Ontario uses straight ones.

title: Double-curve lamp
description: This lamp design with a supporting second curve is only found in Quebec.

title: Wire tags and circles
description: Quebec poles often have a yellow sticker on the lower wire attachment and orange tags. The circle on the upper wire is unique to Quebec.

title: Signs on two posts
description: Quebec likes to hold signs up with two posts.

title: Snowmobile signs
description: Snowmobile crossing signs are most common in Quebec and appear on many northern roads.

title: Metal sign posts in Quebec
description: Quebec uses metal posts for signs far more often than other provinces like Ontario, which uses wood.

title: 'Secteur' on speed signs
description: Some speed signs say 'secteur'. This is unique to Quebec.

title: Minimum speed signs
description: Signs giving a minimum speed under the maximum are unique to Quebec.

title: Quebec highway shields
description: Quebec's autoroutes use a blue and red shield and provincial routes a green one with fleurs-de-lis. Numbers are well organised, so the province is very pinpointable.

title: Red hydrants in Quebec
description: Quebec uses only red-body hydrants. Montreal's have a green top and chains; Quebec City's are plainer.

title: Route 132 on the Gaspé north shore
description: Route 132 along the north of the Gaspé Peninsula is very recognisable: the sea to the north and the large Chic-Choc mountains to the south.

title: Sandy shoulders on Route 138
description: Route 138 along the north shore often has sand on the sides of the road. The sand gets darker to the east and lighter to the west.

title: Route 389 to Labrador
description: Route 389, the northernmost covered road in Quebec, uses only double yellow lines, runs through mountains with exposed rock and has no chevrons, only curve signs. Its spruce trees are some of the most recognisable on Street View.

title: Route 389 near Fermont
description: The northernmost part of Route 389 near Fermont is extremely recognisable: a wet dirt-coloured road found only here, very low trees, a railway alongside and distinctive power lines.

title: Montreal street signs
description: Montreal is easy to identify from the red flower logo on all street signs. Street sign logos are a great way to identify Quebec cities.

title: Montreal compost bins
description: These small brown compost bins with the Montreal logo are specific to Montreal.

title: Yellow hydrant posts
description: Montreal and Gatineau mark hydrants with a yellow post for the snow. Other Quebec cities use a sign-style marker instead.

title: Black sign backs in Montreal
description: Inner Montreal tends to paint the backs of signs black, or sometimes other colours. The outskirts use different colours.

title: Montreal lamp
description: This curved lamp is unique to Montreal.

title: Montreal buses
description: Montreal buses have distinctive coloured chevrons at the back.

title: 'Stop' signs on Mount Royal
description: The Mount Royal area of Montreal uses 'stop' instead of 'arrêt' and has its own street sign.

title: Quebec City street signs
description: Quebec City street signs have no logo but are white with a memorable layout.

title: Old Quebec
description: Downtown Quebec City is known for its European architecture.

title: Blue rectangle on Quebec City hydrant signs
description: A very reliable city meta: every hydrant marker in Quebec City has a blue rectangle on its side.

title: Green buses in Quebec City
description: Quebec City buses are a recognisable green.

title: Red sign backs in L'Ancienne-Lorette
description: The L'Ancienne-Lorette area of Quebec City paints the backs of its signs red.

title: Trois-Rivières street signs
description: Trois-Rivières uses green street signs with a thick white border.

title: Small hydrant markers in Trois-Rivières
description: Trois-Rivières marks hydrants with an extra small yellow square.

title: Gatineau street signs
description: Gatineau street signs are blue with a recognisable oval logo. As a twin city of Ottawa, you will see a mix of Ontario and Quebec plates.

title: Sherbrooke street signs
description: Sherbrooke used green signs with its logo in old coverage; new coverage shows blue signs.

title: Number-only pole tags in Sherbrooke
description: Pole stickers in Sherbrooke and the surroundings only use numbers, without the black 'Q' seen elsewhere in Quebec.

title: Saguenay street signs
description: Saguenay street signs are white and say 'Saguenay' on them.

title: Saguenay hydrant markers
description: Saguenay hydrant markers typically look like this, though a unique alternative design also exists.

title: Granby street signs
description: Granby uses this unique logo on its street signs.

title: 'Stop' signs in Granby
description: The whole city of Granby uses 'stop' signs instead of Quebec's 'arrêt'.

title: Blue hydrant markers in Granby
description: Granby often uses a unique blue hydrant marker.

title: Val-d'Or hydrants
description: Val-d'Or hydrants are red with a blue top and nozzles; street signs are green.

title: British Columbia plates
description: British Columbia has front and rear plates. A very visible registration sticker in the bottom middle tells them apart from Ontario's.

title: BC area codes
description: Vancouver generally uses 604, the rest of British Columbia 250. 778 and 236 can be anywhere.

title: Vancouver Island rainforest
description: The trees on Vancouver Island are taller and denser; parts of the island are temperate rainforest with giant hemlocks and cedars.

title: Cloudy grey west coast towns
description: The coastal towns of western BC have very distinct cloudy, grey and mountainous coverage.

title: Bare light-coloured Rockies
description: The Rockies of southeast BC and southwest Alberta look different from the rest of BC: lighter in colour and with no trees on the tops.

title: Boreal forest of northern BC
description: Northern BC has vast boreal forests of spruce, pine and tamarack, with white aspens. Mountains get smaller to the north.

title: 'km/h' on BC speed signs
description: BC speed limit signs almost always say 'km/h' at the bottom.

title: Common BC pole top
description: This is the most common pole top in British Columbia.

title: Asymmetric 2-1 insulators
description: BC often has asymmetric insulators, two on one side and one on the other, and often tilted ones.

title: Double crossarms
description: BC sometimes has two crossarms close together on one pole.

title: Metal plates on BC poles
description: Small grey or yellow metal rectangles are found on BC poles.

title: Metal circles at the base of poles
description: BC poles often have one to five small metal circles near the base, and sometimes a metal flare at the bottom.

title: BC Hydro boxes
description: Electrical boxes in BC often say 'BC Hydro'.

title: BC hydrant colours
description: Central BC generally uses yellow-body hydrants and the coast and edges red ones. Nozzle colours vary.

title: Solid yellow lights in Vancouver
description: Traffic lights in downtown Vancouver are solid yellow. The rest of BC uses a black middle.

title: Yellow painted curbs
description: BC sometimes paints its curbs yellow, especially on Vancouver Island. Alberta is the only other province that does it commonly.

title: Sea-to-Sky Highway
description: Highway 99 from Vancouver to Whistler: big mountains and water to the west, rugged exposed rock to the east.

title: Smoky Yellowhead Highway
description: A stretch of Highway 16 (Yellowhead) in central BC has distinct smoky coverage from wildfire smoke.

title: Highway 97 in northeastern BC
description: The Alaska Highway section in northeastern BC runs through boreal forest and rolling hills, with very white aspens showing in the Gen 2.

title: Unique pole on Highway 37
description: The southern part of Highway 37 in northwestern BC has this unique pole. There is no Gen 4 in northwestern BC.

title: Bad coverage on Highway 37
description: Most coverage on Highway 37 is really bad, with a huge halo and lots of dirt marks. The mountains are much bigger than on Highway 97.

title: Double white dashes on Highway 77
description: Highway 77 connecting BC to the Northwest Territories always has double white dashes in the middle, with clean Gen 4.

title: Hydrants around Vancouver
description: Vancouver-area hydrants differ by city: white with a blue top in Abbotsford, red in Vancouver, white with red caps in Burnaby.

title: Vancouver buses
description: Vancouver buses have a recognisable design with a blue bottom.

title: Thick sign clasps
description: This thick clasp holding signs to posts is predominantly found in southwestern BC.

title: Chilliwack street signs
description: Chilliwack uses unique coloured street signs with the thick sign clasp.

title: L-shaped signs in Victoria
description: Street signs in Victoria are mostly mounted in an L shape.

title: Esquimalt street signs
description: Esquimalt, next to Victoria, uses its own sign with a recognisable logo.

title: Victoria buses
description: Buses in Victoria have green stripes, unlike Vancouver's blue-bottomed buses. Victoria bus stops are green, sometimes vertical.

title: Nanaimo street signs
description: Nanaimo uses blue street signs with a thick white outline, and yellow curbs.

title: Okanagan orchards
description: Orchards and vineyards are very common around Kelowna; the dry Okanagan can almost look Mediterranean.

title: Kamloops street signs
description: Kamloops uses this green street sign with two bolts on the left side.

title: Kelowna bus stops
description: Kelowna has a lot of these green bus stop signs.

title: Smoky or gloomy Prince George
description: Prince George coverage is either smoky or gloomy and overcast. It is hilly rather than mountainous: a good hedge for smoky coverage.

title: Green lamps in Prince George
description: Prince George likes to use green lamp posts. Its hydrants are yellow.

title: Prince George buses
description: Prince George buses have a recognisable red stripe.

title: Flat Dawson Creek
description: The Dawson Creek region is very flat and looks more like Alberta, with lots of Gen 2, smoky coverage and thin aspens.

title: Smudged Gen 3 around Dawson Creek
description: Most of the Gen 3 around Dawson Creek has a smudge on the camera.

title: Fall coverage around Nelson
description: Southeastern BC around Nelson is mostly fall coverage, where the yellow aspens stand out.

title: Green poles in Nelson
description: The city of Nelson uses unique green sign poles.

title: Totem poles
description: Totem poles are part of the culture of BC's First Nations. They appear at some intersections and in many BC trekkers, and nowhere else in Canada.

title: Follow car in Fort Nelson
description: This car is commonly seen in coverage around Fort Nelson.

title: Boat coverage off Vancouver Island
description: A lot of boat coverage goes around the top of Vancouver Island.

title: Boat coverage in Haida Gwaii
description: A large amount of boat coverage is found in the south of the Haida Gwaii archipelago.

title: Alberta plates
description: Alberta has rear plates only, white with red lettering.

title: Alberta area codes
description: 780 is northern Alberta, 403 the south. 587 and 825 can be anywhere in Alberta.

title: Antenna on mountain dirt roads
description: In the Alberta Rockies, dirt road coverage sometimes shows an antenna. Antennas also appear in some national parks.

title: Montana hills from southern Alberta
description: In the far south of Alberta you can sometimes see isolated hills across the border in Montana.

title: Cypress Hills
description: Southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan share the same dry rolling hills around the Cypress Hills; they can be impossible to tell apart without more clues.

title: Orange buried cable markers
description: Alberta uses a lot of orange buried cable markers and rarely yellow ones. The other prairies also have the orange markers.

title: Alberta three-wire pole top
description: When Alberta poles carry three wires they look like this. Found elsewhere too, but it is the main Alberta pole top.

title: Northern Alberta pole
description: This very distinctive pole with hanging insulators is sometimes found in northern Alberta.

title: Manitoba-like pole without bottom insulator
description: Alberta sometimes has a pole that looks like Manitoba's, but in Alberta one bottom insulator is always missing.

title: Generic guardrails in Alberta
description: Alberta uses generic guardrails more than the other prairies, which more often use some alternative, especially on big roads.

title: Blue Range and Township road signs
description: Rural road signs in Alberta are usually blue and read 'Rge Rd' and 'Twp Rd'. Saskatchewan and Manitoba almost always use green, as do big Alberta cities.

title: Edmonton hydrants
description: Edmonton hydrants are yellow with a blue top and blue nozzles.

title: Red sticker on Edmonton lamp bases
description: A red sticker on the base of a lamp post means you are in Edmonton. About half of them are red, the rest white.

title: Blue transit in Edmonton
description: Edmonton transit uses blue buses, blue stops and blue shelters. The city also has a lot of alleyway coverage.

title: Calgary hydrants
description: Calgary hydrants are pale green with black nozzles.

title: Edmonton and Calgary sign posts
description: Edmonton sign posts have small holes and a cap; Calgary's have no cap and small clasps.

title: Calgary transit
description: Calgary uses dark blue bus stops and red and white buses.

title: Red Deer traffic lights
description: Red Deer, between Calgary and Edmonton, uses black and yellow traffic lights.

title: Red Deer hydrants
description: Red Deer has its own bright green hydrant.

title: Red Deer street signs
description: Red Deer street signs are usually joined horizontally with a small metal strip on the pole side. The city also uses a lot of black lamps.

title: Yellow curbs and sewers
description: Yellow painted curbs and sewers are especially common in Red Deer and many rural Alberta towns.

title: Medicine Hat ridge
description: Medicine Hat has a distinctive ridge to the east and a dry landscape unusual for Alberta.

title: Red hydrants in Medicine Hat and Lethbridge
description: Medicine Hat and Lethbridge use red-body hydrants. Lethbridge's have black nozzles.

title: Medicine Hat street signs
description: Medicine Hat signs often have a connection piece at the bottom, like in Thunder Bay. The city also uses green lamps.

title: Green rural signs around Peace River
description: The Peace River region around Grande Prairie uses green rural road signs, unlike the blue ones in the rest of Alberta.

title: Yellow hydrants in Grande Prairie
description: Grande Prairie is one of the only places in Alberta with yellow hydrants.

title: Full stops on Grande Prairie signs
description: Grande Prairie always puts a full stop at the end of street names.

title: Aquatera bins
description: Garbage bins saying 'Aquatera' are common and unique to Grande Prairie.

title: Highway 35 to the NWT
description: Highway 35 north of Grande Prairie can be identified by its north-western poles, short northern trees and longer grass.

title: Blue street signs in Fort McMurray
description: Fort McMurray is one of the few Alberta cities with blue street signs. Some cities use their own cardinal directions on signs.

title: Brown poles in Fort McMurray
description: Fort McMurray is easily identified by its unique brown lamp poles and the white northern aspens.

title: Dry Highway 63
description: Highway 63 going up to Fort McMurray has a distinctive dry feel.

title: Saskatchewan plates
description: Saskatchewan has rear plates only, white with green lettering.

title: 306 area code
description: The only area code you should see in Saskatchewan is 306.

title: Narrow patched roads
description: Narrow, low-quality patched roads are common in Saskatchewan. Similar Alberta roads are usually wider and in better condition.

title: Tilted camera in southwest Saskatchewan
description: Southwestern Saskatchewan has a lot of tilted-camera coverage.

title: Extra-long crossarm
description: When Saskatchewan poles do not alternate their insulators, the excessive length of the crossarm gives them away.

title: Supported curved lamps
description: About 60% of lamps in Saskatchewan have this curved arm with a support.

title: Green lamp posts in Saskatchewan
description: Saskatchewan loves green lamp posts when they stand alone, away from utility poles.

title: White sign posts
description: White sign posts are particularly common in Saskatchewan. Rural road signs are usually green.

title: Saskatchewan highway shields
description: Saskatchewan's blue highway shields are found on rural roads.

title: Open-loop guardrail ends
description: Saskatchewan guardrails usually have no holes, like Alberta's, and end in an open loop.

title: Saskatoon hydrants
description: Saskatoon hydrants are white with a red top.

title: Regina hydrants
description: Regina hydrants are yellow.

title: Regina and Saskatoon buses
description: Regina buses have a blue stripe; Saskatoon buses have a blue front. Saskatoon bus stops have a distinctive blue sign.

title: Small houses in Saskatchewan
description: Houses in Saskatchewan tend to be smaller than in Alberta, even in the big cities.

title: Holes at the base of Regina posts
description: Saskatoon and Regina sign posts are rectangular without holes, except Regina's have small holes in the bottom few inches.

title: Blue street signs in Regina
description: Regina is the only major Saskatchewan city with blue street signs; Saskatoon uses green.

title: Yellow posts in Estevan
description: Estevan only uses yellow sign posts, basically the only town in Canada that does this, along with yellow hydrants and yellow curbs.

title: Prince Albert hydrants
description: Prince Albert hydrants are red with a blue top; street sign posts are green, other signs sit on thick white posts.

title: Moose Jaw hydrants
description: Moose Jaw hydrants are red with grey nozzles.

title: Moose Jaw transit
description: Moose Jaw's orange MJ Transit bus stop signs.

title: Green wooden lamp posts in Moose Jaw
description: Moose Jaw lamp posts are green-painted wood.

title: Swift Current
description: Swift Current hydrants are red with blue nozzles, traffic lights are black, and the town was covered almost entirely in winter with bare trees.

title: Manitoba plates
description: Manitoba has front and rear plates, with distinctive green triangles on the left and right edges.

title: 204 area code
description: Manitoba uses the 204 area code; 431 was added in 2012.

title: Gravel shoulders
description: Manitoba often has light-coloured gravel on the sides of the road, and gravel ditches instead of white edge lines.

title: Red-tinted Gen 2
description: Manitoba has a lot of Gen 2 coverage with a red tint in the sky.

title: Tall Manitoba poles
description: These tall poles with hanging insulators are pretty much unique to Manitoba. Rural Manitoba poles are very random and switch designs every few poles.

title: Small dark insulators
description: Pole insulators in Manitoba are sometimes smaller, darker and shaped differently than in other provinces.

title: Very long supported lamps
description: An excessively long street lamp with a support is probably Manitoba. Standard Manitoba lamp poles also tend to have a flat wooden top.

title: Green Manitoba lamp
description: This green lamp with a skinny curved support and a pointy top is unique to Manitoba.

title: Metal tags on Manitoba poles
description: Rural pole tags in Manitoba are usually small pieces of metal with a trapezoid under an oval.

title: Large white tags in Winnipeg
description: Winnipeg poles carry large white tags that are very distinctive.

title: Manitoba sign clasp
description: Rural Manitoba towns use this specific sign clasp.

title: Orange snow poles in Winnipeg
description: Winnipeg hydrants always have an orange snow pole beside them.

title: White street signs in Winnipeg
description: Winnipeg street signs are always white.

title: Winnipeg pole attachment
description: This type of sign attachment on poles is unique to Winnipeg.

title: Brandon hydrants
description: Brandon uses rusty pale yellow hydrants, a street sign with its own clasps, and a recognisable bus sign.

title: Black posts in Dauphin
description: Dauphin follows Winnipeg's metas, with the same hydrants and white signs, but always paints its street sign posts black.

title: Thompson
description: Thompson, the northernmost major town of Manitoba, has only overcast Gen 2 with a red-tinted halo, red hydrants, green signs and many green Manitoba lamps.

title: Brown signs in Flin Flon
description: Flin Flon uses brown street signs.

title: Flin Flon smokestack
description: A huge smokestack stands in Flin Flon.

title: Antenna in Churchill
description: Churchill is easy to confuse with northern Nunavut, but its coverage shows an antenna on the right side of the car.

title: Nova Scotia plates
description: Nova Scotia has rear plates only, blue in the middle.

title: 902 area code
description: Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island share the 902 area code. Atlantic Canada often leaves the area code off phone numbers.

title: Treeless northeast Cape Breton
description: The northeast of Cape Breton can lack trees and look like Newfoundland.

title: Main Nova Scotia pole
description: The main Nova Scotia pole has a crossarm much lower and shorter than New Brunswick's, and transformers often at 45 degrees.

title: Stickers wrapped around wires
description: In Nova Scotia it is common to find a sticker wrapped around the wires, usually yellow but sometimes colourful. Sometimes in New Brunswick too.

title: Nova Scotia guardrail
description: Nova Scotia's guardrail sometimes has a second piece of wood long enough to poke out under the rail; New Brunswick's does not. Reflectors on the rail almost always mean Nova Scotia.

title: Yellow tape on concrete dividers
description: Concrete dividers in Nova Scotia often have yellow tape.

title: Snow poles at guardrail ends
description: Nova Scotia often puts sticks, usually yellow snow poles, at the ends of guardrails.

title: Thick rounded borders on signs
description: Thick white borders with curved corners on signs are common in Nova Scotia.

title: Nova Scotia route markers
description: Nova Scotia's arterial highways use a blue shield with the provincial flag, trunk routes a US-style white shield, and secondary routes (200 and above) a brown rectangle.

title: Round posts in Nova Scotia
description: Nova Scotia mostly uses round sign posts; New Brunswick mostly square ones.

title: Green-backed signs with cross beams
description: This green-backed sign held by metal or wooden cross beams is unique to Nova Scotia.

title: Nova Scotia km markers
description: Nova Scotia kilometre markers always show the highway number on top, unlike New Brunswick's.

title: Nova Scotia traffic lights
description: Nova Scotia and New Brunswick use similar lights; New Brunswick has more solid-coloured housings and more vertical lights.

title: Orange hydrants in Halifax
description: Halifax uses unique orange fire hydrants; the rest of Nova Scotia uses red. Dartmouth mixes orange and red ones.

title: Quebec-like pole top in Halifax
description: Within Nova Scotia this pole top is only found in Halifax. It looks a lot like the Quebec one.

title: Flat lamps in Halifax
description: Lamps in Halifax have a distinctive flat head. Black heritage lamps are also very common.

title: Green bollards in Halifax
description: Halifax uses green flexible bollards; cities like Ottawa and Montreal use similar ones in other colours.

title: Halifax buses
description: Halifax buses and bus stops share this blue and yellow colour design.

title: Halifax smokestack
description: This tall smokestack can be seen from many places in Halifax.

title: Sydney pole
description: Sydney has an abundance of this pole; the insulators differ a little from the rare Halifax one. Major Nova Scotia cities sometimes use secondary crossarms.

title: Sydney hydrants
description: A common hydrant in Sydney, red with a snow pole, though many red variations exist.

title: Yellow traffic lights in Sydney
description: Sydney uses the standard yellow Canadian traffic light, which is unusual for Nova Scotia.

title: Sydney bus stops
description: Sydney has a recognisable green CBRM bus stop sign.

title: Yellow hydrants in Yarmouth
description: Most Nova Scotia towns use red hydrants, but Yarmouth uses yellow ones.

title: Amherst hydrants
description: Amherst is another Nova Scotia exception, with pale yellow hydrants.

title: New Brunswick plates
description: New Brunswick plates have red lettering visible through the blur, like Alberta's. Front plates stopped in 2019, so newer coverage shows a mix.

title: 506 area code
description: New Brunswick uses only the 506 area code.

title: Concrete roads without lines
description: New Brunswick has a lot of coverage on concrete roads with no lines.

title: Double insulators
description: Double insulators are more common in New Brunswick than in any other province.

title: Yellow horizontal pole tags
description: New Brunswick poles often have yellow horizontal tags.

title: Long lamp arms
description: Lamp arms are often much longer in New Brunswick than elsewhere.

title: New Brunswick bollards
description: New Brunswick bollards are usually yellow, red or green and more rectangular than the poles found in Quebec or Nova Scotia.

title: Green stickers on sign posts
description: Many signs in New Brunswick have green stickers on their posts.

title: New Brunswick route shields
description: New Brunswick's route shields are unique. Low numbers are major routes; three-digit numbers up into the 900s are secondary routes.

title: Square perforated posts
description: Although Canada is known for wooden posts, New Brunswick mostly uses square metal posts with holes. Prince Edward Island uses only this style.

title: Poles painted as Acadian flags
description: In the Acadian communities of northern New Brunswick it is not uncommon to find poles painted with the Acadian flag.

title: Fredericton hydrants
description: Fredericton uses red hydrants with blue nozzles.

title: Blue street signs in Fredericton
description: Fredericton uses only blue street signs; most of New Brunswick uses green.

title: Rusty posts in Saint John
description: Sign posts in Saint John are almost always extremely rusted and dark.

title: Saint John hydrants
description: Saint John hydrants are red with grey nozzles, marked by a unique L-shaped pole.

title: Saint John buses
description: Saint John buses have a red front.

title: Downtown Saint John
description: Saint John is hillier than the other New Brunswick cities and its downtown has a very European feel.

title: Yellow hydrants in Edmundston
description: Edmundston is the only major New Brunswick city with yellow hydrants, with grey nozzles. It also likes a pole that is rare in the province.

title: Red snow poles in Moncton
description: Moncton always has red snow poles beside its hydrants.

title: Moncton street signs
description: Street signs in Moncton sometimes carry this logo.

title: Moncton tower
description: This large tower is visible from many places in Moncton, which is much flatter than the other New Brunswick cities.

title: Prince Edward Island plates
description: Prince Edward Island has rear plates only.

title: Main PEI pole
description: The most common pole on Prince Edward Island, a mix of the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia poles.

title: Eastern PEI pole
description: This pole is unique to Prince Edward Island and dominant in the east of the island. Do not confuse it with Ontario.

title: Bilingual signs in PEI
description: Prince Edward Island has some bilingualism, mostly in the west around Summerside. Street signs can be bilingual, but stop signs are not.

title: Green-backed place name signs
description: Most place name signs in Prince Edward Island have green backs. Also common in British Columbia, sometimes Nova Scotia.

title: PEI route marker
description: Prince Edward Island's route marker, a green shield with trees. Route signage is less consistently bilingual than in New Brunswick.

title: Asymmetric poles in Charlottetown
description: Charlottetown uses a lot of asymmetric poles like these.

title: Horizontal lights in Charlottetown
description: Charlottetown uses horizontal black traffic lights, like Quebec.

title: Charlottetown smokestacks
description: Charlottetown has several recognisable grey smokestacks. The red dirt is less obvious in the city than elsewhere on the island.

title: Summerside street signs
description: Summerside has unique blue street signs on curled brackets. Bilingual signs are much more common here than in Charlottetown.

title: Summerside hydrants
description: Summerside hydrants have white nozzles and always a red snow pole; Charlottetown's have grey nozzles.

title: Yellow pole tags in Summerside
description: Summerside uses yellow pole tags like New Brunswick; the rest of the island uses the white one.

title: Stars on the wires
description: Summerside has unique star-shaped markers on its wires, sometimes seen in Nova Scotia.

title: Confederation Bridge
description: This huge bridge with a hump in the middle is the Confederation Bridge linking Prince Edward Island to New Brunswick.

title: Newfoundland and Labrador plates
description: Newfoundland and Labrador has rear plates only, sometimes with a visible orange registration sticker. Pickup trucks, heavy vehicles, buses and government vehicles do carry front plates.

title: 709 area code
description: Both Newfoundland and Labrador use the 709 area code.

title: Barren southern peninsulas
description: The far south of Newfoundland is very recognisable for its barren, dry landscape. The south in general looks drier with fewer trees.

title: Southwest Newfoundland mountains
description: The southwest of Newfoundland has distinctive mountains and its own pole.

title: Gloomy fall coverage in the northeast
description: Gloomy fall coverage is found in northeastern Newfoundland and is easy to confuse with other provinces.

title: Main Newfoundland pole
description: The most common pole in Newfoundland: double crossarms with thick insulators.

title: Second Newfoundland pole top
description: The second most common pole top in Newfoundland.

title: Southwest Newfoundland pole
description: This pole top with widely spaced insulators is found in the southwest; a similar one with closer insulators exists across the island.

title: Wooden boxes at pole bases
description: Many poles in Newfoundland have a wooden box at the bottom.

title: Top-heavy insulators in the east
description: Insulators whose top part is larger than the bottom are most common in eastern Newfoundland.

title: Newfoundland route signs
description: Newfoundland routes are shown as a black number in a white square on a big green sign. Primary routes end in 0; branches carry other numbers. The word 'ROUTE' on signs is found in no other province.

title: Route numbers by region
description: Newfoundland route numbers follow regions: 1-2 digits and 100s on the Avalon, 200s in the east, 300s around Gander, 400s in the west and Northern Peninsula, 500s in Labrador.

title: 'Line' roads
description: In Newfoundland a 'line' is a long inter-community road, a term used almost nowhere else.

title: Round posts with rear clasps
description: Newfoundland sign posts are usually round with clasps on the back of the signs.

title: Orange sign backs
description: Some signs in Newfoundland have orange-looking backs.

title: Viking Trail markers
description: Route 430, the Viking Trail, has markers with a Viking longboat; older ones every 30-40 km show the distance from Deer Lake.

title: St. John's taxis
description: St. John's has a very recognisable orange taxi.

title: Yellow hydrants in St. John's
description: Within Newfoundland, yellow hydrants are unique to St. John's, and so is the diamond on their marker.

title: Mount Pearl street signs
description: Mount Pearl, part of the St. John's area, has its own blue street sign.

title: Street signs north of St. John's
description: North of St. John's, towns use this unique dark blue street sign.

title: Mount Pearl hydrants
description: Mount Pearl has its own green hydrant design.

title: Numbered hydrants in Corner Brook
description: Corner Brook marks all its hydrants with numbers. The city sits on a large hill, which usually gives it away.

title: Gander hydrant markers
description: Gander uses a unique yellow hydrant marker instead of the diamond.

title: Gander street signs
description: Gander uses white street signs, sometimes with bold black text.

title: Happy Valley-Goose Bay
description: Happy Valley-Goose Bay, the largest town in Labrador, was covered in Gen 4 on a gloomy November day with ridges in the distance. Very short lamps, light-coloured flat-roofed buildings.

title: North West River bridge
description: A unique bridge connects North West River to Sheshatshiu, just north of Happy Valley-Goose Bay. Both towns use a guardrail without the prism posts.

title: North West River street signs
description: North West River has its own green street sign.

title: Churchill Falls
description: Churchill Falls was covered on a nice day with green grass, distinctive hills to the east, a unique lamp at every house and Halloween decorations.

title: Wabush red-lettered signs
description: The single road of coverage in Wabush has red-lettered signs visible from all locations, and rainy weather.

title: Torngat Mountains trekker
description: A distinct trekker in Torngat Mountains National Park, at the very north of Labrador.

title: Yukon plates
description: Yukon has rear plates only.

title: 867 area code
description: All three northern territories use the 867 area code.

title: Fireweed
description: Pink fireweed is mostly found in southern Yukon. It shows best in Gen 2; in Gen 4 it looks darker.

title: Autumn Gen 4 in Yukon
description: Yukon's Gen 4 was captured in September, giving yellow and orange autumn colours. Yukon has only Gen 2 and Gen 4.

title: Orange-tinted Yukon poles
description: Most Yukon poles are generic but often have a dark orange tint.

title: Complicated crossarms
description: Yukon poles often have complicated crossarm arrangements.

title: Yukon highway signs
description: Standard Yukon highway guide signs, with route numbers in a square.

title: White posts on Yukon highways
description: Yukon highway sign posts are generally white, and the backs of signs look like this.

title: White borders on rural road names
description: Rural street name signs in Yukon generally have white borders; small road signs usually have an arrow.

title: Guardrails in Yukon
description: Yukon generally uses guardrails where British Columbia uses concrete blocks.

title: Sunset Gen 4 near Watson Lake
description: All the Gen 4 on the Alaska Highway east of Watson Lake has a very bright sunset to the east. Further west the highway is cloudy Gen 2 only.

title: Orange-topped snow poles
description: This part of the Alaska Highway west of Watson Lake has a lot of orange-topped snow poles.

title: Rancheria valley
description: This section of the Alaska Highway runs in a valley with the Rancheria River to the south, with quite a lot of fireweed.

title: Teslin Lake
description: Teslin Lake is visible to the southwest on this segment of the Alaska Highway.

title: Dark insulators from Johnsons Crossing
description: From Johnsons Crossing to Marsh Lake the Alaska Highway is lined with this pole top with dark insulators.

title: Extra crossarm past Marsh Lake
description: Past Marsh Lake towards Whitehorse another crossarm is added to the poles along the Alaska Highway.

title: Snow poles near Haines Junction
description: This section of the Alaska Highway from Haines Junction to Silver City has these snow poles. Huge mountains in the distance and stronger autumn colours.

title: No edge lines near Silver City
description: Approaching Silver City the Alaska Highway gets wider and loses its white edge lines.

title: Kluane Lake
description: Kluane Lake, always to the east of the Alaska Highway between Silver City and Burwash Landing, is probably the most recognisable lake in Yukon. One of the most common roads to get.

title: Destruction Bay
description: The Gen 2 around Destruction Bay is especially common: the lake in view, booming fireweed and the town's lamps make it pinpointable.

title: Pole north of Destruction Bay
description: This standard pole top runs north from Destruction Bay to Burwash Landing. There are no poles south of Destruction Bay.

title: Barren Quill Creek
description: Past Kluane Lake towards Quill Creek the landscape is barren: bushes and fireweed, shorter and sparser trees, dark bare mountains.

title: Bad weather south of Whitehorse
description: The Klondike Highway south of Whitehorse is Gen 2 only with cloudy, bad weather, worse on the BC side of the border than in Yukon.

title: Fireweed and wooden guardrail on BC's Klondike
description: On the BC part of the Klondike Highway you find dark fireweed and a wooden-post guardrail, both unusual for BC.

title: Bollards on BC's Klondike
description: Various bollards and snow poles are found on the BC side of the Klondike Highway, not in Yukon.

title: Dry road from Carcross
description: From Carcross to the Alaska Highway junction the weather is still cloudy but the landscape feels drier.

title: Dry July Gen 2 on the Klondike
description: The Gen 2 between Whitehorse and Dawson City was taken in July, making it some of the driest Yukon coverage.

title: Sun glare from Pelly Crossing
description: All the Gen 4 from Pelly Crossing to Dawson City has a huge sun glare to the south.

title: Haines Highway
description: The Haines Highway has cloudy, bad-weather Gen 2, with Gen 4 on its northern part. Fireweed is common on the Yukon part, nearly absent in BC.

title: Haines Highway snow pole
description: This unique snow pole is found all along the Haines Highway, the most consistent snow pole meta in Yukon.

title: Gravel Campbell Highway
description: Between Watson Lake and Ross River the Robert Campbell Highway is mostly gravel, with a bright sun to the southeast in Gen 4.

title: Paved north Campbell Highway
description: The north part of the Campbell Highway has the same southeast sun but is paved without white edge lines.

title: Square blur on the Campbell Highway
description: All the Gen 2 on the Campbell Highway is cloudy, with a square blur on the front right of the camera and dirt spots.

title: White car from Ross River to Faro
description: Yukon uses a blue Gen 4 car, but between Ross River and Faro the car can appear white.

title: Southern Dempster Highway
description: The south of the Dempster Highway, before Tombstone park, is lined with short shrubby trees under a cloudy, ominous sky.

title: Dempster valleys
description: Most of the Dempster Highway is a small gravel road in valleys with distinct red and yellow colours.

title: Square blur in Tombstone park
description: Only within Tombstone Territorial Park, a square blur appears on the front right of the camera on the Dempster.

title: Snow poles on the Yukon Dempster
description: On the Yukon side of the Dempster you find snow poles or nothing; the NWT side almost always has a white bollard.

title: Second Google car on the Dempster
description: A second Google car can be seen following in many locations on the Dempster Highway.

title: Narrow Canol Road
description: The Canol Road has only spotty Gen 2. It is very narrow and lined with light-coloured vegetation; the south is sunny, sometimes in an open valley.

title: Canol Road snow pole
description: This snow pole is often seen on the southern part of the Canol Road.

title: Rain at Quiet Lake
description: The Quiet Lake section of the Canol Road is identifiable by rain coverage and a jungle-like vegetation.

title: Stormy Lapie River section
description: Near the Lapie River bridge the Canol Road has unique mountainous coverage with stormy weather, some of the most extreme weather on Street View.

title: Canol Road north of Ross River
description: North of Ross River the Canol Road is still narrow with similar vegetation but sunnier, and gets close to the water near the river.

title: Tagish Road
description: Tagish Road, linking the Alaska and Klondike highways, has cloudy Gen 2 only and no white edge lines. Raindrops on the camera increase to the east.

title: Orange dirt near the Alaska border
description: On the Top of the World Highway the dirt gets very orange close to the Alaska border.

title: Whitehorse street signs
description: Whitehorse street signs are green with a unique symbol.

title: Rusty lamps in Whitehorse
description: Lamps in Whitehorse are rusted to a dark brown, though some have been replaced with silver or yellow ones.

title: Whitehorse hydrants
description: Whitehorse hydrants are yellow with black nozzles.

title: Whitehorse garbage bins
description: Whitehorse garbage bins have a white horse symbol.

title: Downtown Whitehorse lamps
description: Decorative double lamps in downtown Whitehorse.

title: Whitehorse pole top
description: Although found elsewhere in Yukon, this pole top is most common in and around Whitehorse.

title: Hoodoos around Whitehorse
description: Large rocky ridges surround Whitehorse, with hoodoo rock formations.

title: Foggy blur in Whitehorse
description: All Gen 4 in Whitehorse has a distinct foggy blur on the front left of the camera.

title: Dawson City street signs
description: Dawson City has unique white street signs on black posts.

title: Dawson City hydrants
description: Dawson City hydrants are yellow.

title: Dawson City valley
description: Dawson City is built in a huge valley surrounded by mountains, though much of its coverage is foggy.

title: Frontier architecture in Dawson City
description: Dawson City has colourful frontier-style wooden buildings.

title: Foggy entrance to Dawson City
description: The Klondike Highway entering Dawson City from the east has fog in every direction, which makes it unique.

title: Pole from Dawson City to the airport
description: This unique pole runs on the south side of the road from Dawson City to the airport.

title: 2009 coverage around Dawson City
description: Roads around Dawson City have July 2009 coverage that looks extremely dry with a warm tinge and very white birches.

title: Watson Lake lamps
description: All Watson Lake locations on the Alaska Highway have these blue-green lamps, many with flags.

title: Sign Post Forest
description: The Sign Post Forest in Watson Lake.

title: Haines Junction mountains
description: Haines Junction is best identified by the large mountain range to the southwest. The town is built on a slope, uphill to the north.

title: Haines Junction hydrants
description: Two hydrant types are found in Haines Junction: red with yellow caps and yellow.

title: Haines Junction street signs
description: Haines Junction's official wooden street signs; only about ten exist, some replaced by standard Yukon signs.

title: Carmacks street signs
description: Carmacks street signs are wooden like Haines Junction's but on brown posts. All transformers in Carmacks sit at 45 degrees.

title: Carmacks
description: Carmacks lies on the Yukon River surrounded by hills, with only Gen 2 in town. The Gen 4 on the Klondike Highway through it has yellow lamps and a distinct hill.

title: Ross River ridge
description: Ross River has only cloudy Gen 2 with a large distinct ridge to the north. It uses standard Yukon street signs and yield signs instead of stops.

title: Faro
description: Faro has limited Gen 4 only, with a bright sunset and a medium-sized hill to the north. Its street signs are unique.

title: Teslin
description: Teslin, on the Alaska Highway, has Gen 2 only with a distinct hill to the northwest. All its lamps carry the same flags.

title: Carcross
description: Carcross has cloudy Gen 2 only, surrounded by big mountains and water: Nares Lake to the east and Bennett Lake to the west.

title: Mayo
description: Mayo has Gen 2 only with a hill to the south.

title: Pole on the road to Mayo
description: This unique pole is visible on the north side of the road connecting Mayo to the Klondike Highway.

title: Bilingual signs in Pelly Crossing
description: Pelly Crossing has bilingual street signs. The Pelly River Bridge is visible from all locations.

title: Upper Liard lamps
description: Upper Liard has Gen 2 only, with grey lamps on the north side of the road; the Liard bridge is visible in the distance.

title: Road to Tungsten
description: The road to Tungsten has orange autumn colours and a huge blur to the east in the south, shorter trees in large valleys in the middle, and gets mountainous at the NWT end.

title: Nisutlin Bay Bridge
description: The Nisutlin Bay Bridge at Teslin on the Alaska Highway, the longest bridge in Yukon. Gen 2 only.

title: Teslin River Bridge
description: The Teslin River Bridge at Johnsons Crossing on the Alaska Highway.

title: Tagish Bridge
description: The Tagish Bridge on Tagish Road.

title: Donjek River Bridge
description: The Donjek River Bridge on the Alaska Highway, over a mostly dry riverbed.

title: Carmacks Bridge
description: The bridge over the Yukon River at Carmacks on the Klondike Highway.

title: Pelly River Bridge
description: The Pelly River Bridge at Pelly Crossing on the Klondike Highway.

title: Upper Liard bridge
description: The bridge at Upper Liard on the Alaska Highway.

title: Pelly River crossing near Faro
description: The bridge over the Pelly River near Faro and Ross River.

title: White River crossing
description: The White River bridge on the Alaska Highway near Beaver Creek.

title: Northwest Territories plates
description: The Northwest Territories have rear plates only, shaped like a polar bear.

title: Flat NWT
description: The Northwest Territories are mostly flat, unlike mountainous Yukon, with tall thin boreal trees. Coverage is limited to a few southern roads and the Dempster.

title: Exposed rock north of Great Slave Lake
description: Within the Northwest Territories, exposed rock on the roadside is only found north of Great Slave Lake, on the north part of Highway 3.

title: White posts in the NWT
description: Many signs in the Northwest Territories sit on white posts.

title: Eastern Highway 1
description: The east of NWT Highway 1, from the Alberta border to the Highway 3 junction, has Gen 4 and Gen 2; the Gen 2 shows smudges on the front of the car.

title: Highway 1 bollard
description: This bollard is found randomly on the east part of NWT Highway 1.

title: Green posts near Heart Lake
description: On Highway 1, green posts are only found near Heart Lake. Green poles also appear on north Highway 3, but that road is Gen 2 only.

title: Unpaved western Highway 1
description: The west part of NWT Highway 1 is Gen 4 only and unpaved, flatter than the similar gravel part of Highway 7.

title: Western Highway 1 bollard
description: This bollard is sometimes found on the west part of NWT Highway 1.

title: Paved section near Fort Simpson
description: A small paved section of Highway 1 near Fort Simpson has a large sunset to the east and generic poles on the east side.

title: Pilot car
description: A 'pilot car' is seen in front of the Google car on a section of NWT Highway 1.

title: Highway 3
description: NWT Highway 3 towards Yellowknife has Gen 2 only. Its northern part is open and rocky, with a more significant smudge on the camera.

title: Highway 3 bollard
description: This bollard is found a lot on north Highway 3. Its black bands are closer together than Alberta's.

title: Green posts towards Yellowknife
description: Green, sometimes grey, posts and lamps line the north part of Highway 3 towards Yellowknife.

title: Paved southern Highway 7
description: NWT Highway 7 is only paved for a small southern section, then under construction to Fort Liard.

title: Gravel Highway 7
description: After Fort Liard Highway 7 narrows to gravel up to Highway 1, hillier than the similar gravel part of Highway 1.

title: Bollards on the NWT Dempster
description: The western, hilly part of the Dempster (Highway 8) in the NWT can almost always be identified by these bollards; the Yukon side uses snow poles.

title: Foggy hills on the NWT Dempster
description: The western hilly part of NWT Highway 8 has the red and yellow Dempster colours but extra fog. The rest is flat Gen 2 with improving weather northwards.

title: Green lamps in Yellowknife
description: Green lamps are the main feature of Yellowknife; Whitehorse uses dark brown.

title: Garbage boxes in Yellowknife
description: Garbage boxes stand in front of many driveways in Yellowknife, a bit like in Newfoundland.

title: Raindrops in Yellowknife
description: Yellowknife has Gen 2 only, and raindrops on the camera are unique to it.

title: Yellowknife hydrants
description: Hydrants are not common in Yellowknife, but they look like this: red with a silver top.

title: Yellowknife street signs
description: Yellowknife street signs are plain green; Whitehorse often adds a horse symbol.

title: Red sky in Inuvik
description: Inuvik shows up a lot on Canada maps. Its weather is gloomy and the sky has an extremely red tint.

title: Garbage crates in Inuvik
description: Garbage crates stand at the end of many driveways in Inuvik, like in Yellowknife.

title: Yellow guardrails in Inuvik
description: Inuvik should be the only place with yellow guardrails, along with this bollard.

title: Fort McPherson
description: Fort McPherson looks like Inuvik but with clear blue skies, and has its own hydrant design.

title: Enterprise lanes
description: Enterprise is best identified by its asymmetric 2-1 lanes and various bollards.

title: Fort Liard main street
description: The one road of coverage in Fort Liard can be identified by yellow pole tags and green signs. NWT lamps have a Quebec-like curve, here tilted slightly upwards.

title: Fort Simpson guardrail reflectors
description: Fort Simpson has many guardrails, all with NWT reflectors. Its landscape could easily be confused with other provinces.

title: Tulita antenna
description: Tulita can be identified by the front of the car and its antenna; often only the antenna is visible. Brown dirt, overcast skies and short trees.

title: Iqaluit hydrants
description: Hydrants in Iqaluit are unique, surrounded by red bollards. All Iqaluit coverage is snowy and it is a trekker, so the camera is on the roadside.

title: Road from Iqaluit to Apex
description: The road between Iqaluit and Apex can be identified by its orange and green markers and poles.

title: Dog sled near Iqaluit
description: Dog sled coverage is found just south of Iqaluit.

title: Boat south of Qikiqtarjuaq
description: A large amount of boat coverage lies south of Qikiqtarjuaq.

title: Resolute airport road
description: The road to the airport in Resolute has generic poles to the west and snow poles.

title: Cambridge Bay airport road
description: Cambridge Bay coverage is wet and overcast. The road to the airport has poles on one side and this snow pole on the other; the cemetery road has water to the southeast.

title: Cambridge Bay trekkers
description: Three trekkers across the river at Cambridge Bay: the Maud, the old stone church and the old town.

title: Red quad bike in Grise Fiord
description: Looking down in Grise Fiord, the corner of a red quad bike is visible from most locations.

title: Snowmobile on the Belcher Islands
description: There is a huge amount of snowmobile coverage around the northern Belcher Islands; north of Sanikiluaq the mirrors are visible.

title: Belcher Islands coat
description: This trekker in the south Belcher Islands shows a unique coat.

title: Expedition near Ellef Ringnes Island
description: A trekker south of Ellef Ringnes Island shows a hiking expedition with dogs, sleds and a snowmobile.

title: Quttinirpaaq National Park
description: A trekker on Ellesmere Island in Quttinirpaaq National Park, the northernmost coverage in the world, with a large glacier in a desolate landscape.
